clue.text: Stage construction (and deconstruction) by

parts.note: to make something is to construct it
taken as written, the bracketed word
to break something is to take it apart, the opposite of building

explanation.surface: A theatre piece that is built up and then torn down, credited to an author whose name the print has lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held ends 'by', cut short: the setter meant 'by 28', the playwright at 28 across, who wrote a play of this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage here stands for a theatre play, and Make and Break is a comedy written for the theatre.

clue.text: Roald Dahl's child heroine recalls Drayton's' "Empress"

explanation.surface: A famous children's book heroine shares her name with an empress from an Elizabethan poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empress Matilda was the twelfth-century claimant to the English throne; Drayton, an Elizabethan poet, wrote verse on a Matilda.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahl's clever schoolgirl bears this name, and Michael Drayton's poem The Legend of Matilda concerns a royal lady of the same name.

clue.text: Murdoch's little German girl

parts.note: a heroine from an Iris Murdoch novel whose surname is the German word for small

explanation.surface: A novelist's small German daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Honor Klein is the enigmatic woman in Iris Murdoch's A Severed Head; her surname is German for 'little'.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the half-sister in A Severed Head is also the German adjective meaning small.

clue.text: … with his chin he drove / The bristled lips before him " (Coriolanus)

definitions.text: … with his chin he drove / The bristled lips before him " (Coriolanus)

parts.words: … with his chin he drove / The bristled lips before him " (Coriolanus)
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's Coriolanus with one adjective left out before the word chin; supply it

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare quotation about a beardless young warrior with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Cominius recalls the young Coriolanus fighting 'with his Amazonian chin', smooth as a woman warrior's.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing epithet likens the hairless chin to that of the warrior women of Greek legend.

clue.text: African queen's antic

explanation.surface: A North African monarch is a clown.
explanation.definitionFit: Dido was the legendary queen of Carthage, and 'cutting a dido' is an old phrase for playing a prank or caper.

clue.text: Finnish writer puts old letter on ice

parts.note: a rune is a letter of the ancient Germanic alphabet
a berg is a mass of floating ice

explanation.surface: A Finnish author carves an ancient character on a glacier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts ... on' places the old letter first, on top of the ice in a down clue. Johan Ludvig Runeberg is Finland's national poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Runeberg wrote Finland's national anthem and is the country's most celebrated poet.

clue.text: Scott protagonist in a very black book

parts.note: BB marks a very soft, very black pencil lead
OT is the Old Testament, a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A hero of Walter Scott's turns up in a dark and sinister volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The Abbot is a Walter Scott novel; its title figure is the abbot of Kennaquhair.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scott novel takes its title from its central figure, the head of a monastery.

clue.text: Hail a hat turned inside out by Racine

indicators.note: a hat turned inside out is thoroughly rearranged, so the letters of the three words are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A greeting to a hat worn reversed by a French dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Racine's tragedy Athalie is known in English by the biblical queen's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Racine's last tragedy is about the Old Testament queen of that name, so the title is a work by the dramatist.

clue.text: Not the best justifier of God's ways, Housman thought

definitions.text: Not the best justifier of God's ways, Housman thought

parts.words: Not the best justifier of God's ways, Housman thought
parts.note: Housman wrote that malt does more than a certain poet can to justify God's ways to man; name that poet

explanation.surface: A poet judged a weaker theologian than beer.
explanation.walkthrough: In A Shropshire Lad Housman says 'malt does more than Milton can / To justify God's ways to man', echoing Paradise Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Paradise Lost set out to justify the ways of God to men, and Housman mocked the attempt.

clue.text: Retreat after the conflict in barchester

indicators.note: the retreat comes after the other pieces in the answer

parts.note: taken as written
war is armed conflict
a den is a private retreat or study

explanation.surface: Someone withdraws to safety once fighting ends in a cathedral town.
explanation.walkthrough: Barchester is Trollope's imaginary cathedral city; The Warden is the first Barsetshire novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's first Barsetshire novel is set in the cathedral city, so the definition points to a book located there.

clue.text: Home girl has flutter on unknown ego

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Home girl has flutter on unknown ego (5)' for BETTI: BET (flutter) and I (ego) fit, but no standard reading makes 'unknown' give T, and 'Home girl' does not clearly define the Italian playwright; likely OCR damage.
annotationWithheld.clue: Home girl has flutter on unknown ego

clue.text: Property alternative for illusory interlocutor

parts.note: land is real estate, property
or is the word that introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: Choosing between an estate and something else for an imaginary conversation partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Savage Landor wrote Imaginary Conversations, dialogues with invented speakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Landor's Imaginary Conversations are dialogues he invented between historical figures, making him the writer of fanciful talk.

clue.text: Quickly remove what's not representational

explanation.surface: Swiftly taking away anything that is not figurative art.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstract is to take away or filch, and abstract art depicts no recognisable objects.

clue.text: And full as craving too and full (Dryden, All for Love)

definitions.text: And full as craving too and full (Dryden, All for Love)

parts.words: And full as craving too and full (Dryden, All for Love)
parts.note: a line from Dryden's tragedy All for Love whose last two words are left off; supply them

explanation.surface: A quotation from Dryden's Antony and Cleopatra play, cut off before its end.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line is 'And full as craving too, and full as vain', on Antony's appetite.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing ending completes Dryden's line, with vain meaning empty or futile.

clue.text: French satirist a roué, we hear

definitions.text: French satirist a roué, we hear

parts.words: French satirist a roué, we hear
parts.note: spoken quickly, the words a roue echo the family name of a French satirist, born Francois-Marie Arouet

explanation.surface: Rumour has it a French satirical writer was a rake.
explanation.walkthrough: Voltaire's real name was François-Marie Arouet; 'a roué' said aloud gives that surname, so the clue is wit rather than wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Candide adopted a pen name; his birth surname sounds like the phrase in the clue.

clue.text: Sort of nasty outbreak in the Indies chronicled in Winchester

definitions.text: Sort of nasty outbreak in the Indies chronicled in Winchester

parts.words: Sort of nasty outbreak in the Indies chronicled in Winchester
parts.note: a skin outbreak, but also the volcanic event in the East Indies that Simon Winchester described

explanation.surface: A disease epidemic in the colonies recorded in an English cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: Winchester looks like the city but is the author Simon Winchester, whose book Krakatoa tells of the 1883 volcanic blast in the East Indies.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash breaking out on the skin and a volcano blowing up share this name.

clue.text: Polka I devised cancelled for playwright

indicators.note: something devised is newly put together, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: an event called off is cancelled

explanation.surface: A dance routine is invented and then scrapped for a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devised' reworks POLKA I into POLIAK. Stephen Poliakoff is an English playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Poliakoff writes stage and television drama.

clue.text: Geoff, say, hath, perhaps, biblical connections to judge

indicators.note: say signals that the name is to be spoken and spelt to match how it sounds

parts.note: a man's name, pronounced like the first syllable needed

indicators.note: perhaps marks the following word as one to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man named Geoff has, maybe, links in Scripture to a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns HATH into THAH. 'biblical connections to' says the pieces join to make a Bible name; Jephthah was one of the judges of Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: Jephthah led Israel in the Book of Judges, so he counts among its judges.

clue.text: Novelist in carousal in Germany

indicators.note: the first in says the name lies inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A writer is caught up in a drinking spree while visiting Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: J D Salinger wrote The Catcher in the Rye.
explanation.definitionFit: J D Salinger was an American writer of fiction.

clue.text: Inscrutable subject of Wilde

parts.note: an enigmatic creature that is the topic of one of Oscar Wilde's long poems

explanation.surface: A mysterious topic chosen by Oscar Wilde.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde's poem The Sphinx addresses the riddling creature of legend.
explanation.definitionFit: The riddling monster of Egyptian and Greek legend is a byword for an unreadable face, and Wilde wrote a poem to it.

clue.text: Girl for whom Lovelace turned a lathe

indicators.note: turned, a woodworking word beside lathe, signals the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet works at his woodturning machine for his sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace wrote 'To Althea, from Prison' ('Stone walls do not a prison make').
explanation.definitionFit: The Cavalier poet Lovelace addressed a famous lyric to a woman of this name.

clue.text: Joy of the lioness

parts.note: Joy is a first name: the woman who raised the lioness Elsa and wrote Born Free

explanation.surface: The delight a big cat takes.
explanation.walkthrough: Joy looks like a feeling, but it is Joy Adamson, who raised Elsa the lioness.
explanation.definitionFit: Joy Adamson told the story of Elsa the lioness in Born Free.

clue.text: Brave (New World), of Superior breeding

parts.note: a Native American warrior raised by the shore of Lake Superior, hero of Longfellow's poem

explanation.surface: Huxley's novel and a well-bred upper-class person.
explanation.walkthrough: Brave is a Native American warrior, New World is America, and Superior is the Great Lake by which Longfellow's hero grew up, not a mark of class.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's poem is about an Ojibwe hero raised on the shores of Gitche Gumee, Lake Superior.

clue.text: He was successfully on the fiddle in Cremona ()

definitions.text: He was successfully on the fiddle in Cremona ()

parts.words: He was successfully on the fiddle in Cremona ()
parts.note: not a swindler but a member of a famous violin-making family of the Italian town

explanation.surface: An Italian made a good living from fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: On the fiddle means cheating in British slang; here it is literal, about the Amati family who made violins in Cremona.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amati family made the earliest great violins in Cremona.

clue.text: Squeamish reaction by Sartre

explanation.surface: Feeling queasy when reading an existentialist.
explanation.definitionFit: Queasiness is the feeling of wanting to vomit, and La Nausée is Sartre's first novel.

clue.text: Provenance of 8's damsels who lamented the fate of Thammuz

definitions.text: Provenance of 8's damsels who lamented the fate of Thammuz

parts.words: Provenance of 8's damsels who lamented the fate of Thammuz
parts.note: in Paradise Lost, by the poet at 8 down, the damsels mourning Thammuz come from a Middle Eastern land

explanation.surface: Where the mourning women in a Milton epic come from.
explanation.walkthrough: Paradise Lost Book I: Thammuz, 'whose annual wound in Lebanon allured / The Syrian damsels to lament his fate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton calls the mourners of Thammuz Syrian, naming the country they came from.

clue.text: George Russell includes afterthought for church feature

indicators.note: includes means one piece holds the other within it

parts.note: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George William Russell
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: An Irish poet adds a postscript about a part of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: George Russell, the Irish mystic poet, signed himself AE.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the vaulted recess at the east end of a church.

clue.text: Bellini work is the average article

parts.note: the norm is the average or usual standard
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An opera by Bellini is just an ordinary piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Norma is Bellini's best-known opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Norma is an opera composed by Bellini.

clue.text: Spiced wine, or Sapphic cocktail

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters of the two words are mixed

explanation.surface: Mulled wine, or a drink mixed for a poet of Lesbos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocktail' mixes OR SAPPHIC. Hippocras is medieval wine sweetened and spiced.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippocras was a medieval drink of wine with sugar and spices.

clue.text: He was responsible for those at play

definitions.text: He was responsible for those at play

parts.words: He was responsible for those at play
parts.note: not a supervisor of children but the dramatist who wrote the farce about actors, Noises Off

explanation.surface: A man in charge of the children playing.
explanation.walkthrough: Those at play are actors: the writer of Noises Off, a farce about a touring company, put them on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The English dramatist wrote Noises Off, a comedy about a troupe of actors.
